new_statements.quote: Stress is realised in Kaure as intensity and tone, but not as length. Primary stress is distinguished from secondary stress by a higher intensity only. Stress is always on the syllable that phonetically either has a high level tone or a high-mid falling tone. Nonetheless, stress is only partly predictable. In any utterance that has a phonemic high-mid falling tone on one syllable, the stress always goes to that syllable. In any utterance that has a phonemic syllable sequence of two high-mid falling tones, the stress goes to the first syllable of the sequence. [...] However, stress on syllables with phonemic high tones is not predictable in Kaure, and it is therefore phonemic. [...] The main word stress of the extended phonological word is always on the last stressed syllable.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Kaure has two phonemic tones (high level, high-mid fall). Stress (intensity) always sits on a syllable bearing one of these tones, and is driven by the falling tone: a word/utterance with one falling-tone syllable stresses that syllable; two adjacent falling tones -> stress on the first; several non-adjacent falling tones -> primary stress on the last, secondary on the others. Where no falling tone decides it (only high-level tones), stress position is unpredictable, i.e. lexical. In affixed (extended) phonological words the main stress is on the last stressed syllable. StressTyp2 codes it as an unbounded, right-oriented lexical/tone-conditioned system; WALS 14A 'No fixed stress', 15A 'Unbounded: stress can be anywhere', 16A 'Prominence', 17A 'Trochaic'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Per the quoted passage, all non-final falling-tone syllables take secondary stress, and an affixed phonological word can carry up to four secondary-stressed syllables; primary differs from secondary by intensity only. StressTyp2's own Remarks add: secondary stress on alternating syllables preceding the primary, falling-tone syllables always secondary-stressed (unless directly before the primary), no degenerate feet.
new_statements.exceptions: Sequences of three falling tones not encountered; stress on syllables with only high-level tone is unpredictable/phonemic; StressTyp2 lists a separate 'Exceptional (Kaure)' pattern (id 789) with no details.
new_statements.domain_note: Dommel & Dommel phrase the rules over the 'utterance' and the '(extended) phonological word' (up to 15 syllables); no citation-form caveat given. Reported for the Harna/Masta dialect of Kaure, not for the Narau variety itself. The primary paper was NOT opened; the quotation comes from StressTyp2's Sources passage, which attributes it to pp. 3, 5-6.
new_statements.identity_note: nara1265 is a Glottolog "Bookkeeping" languoid. ISO 639-3 change request 2019-030 (adopted 2020-01-23; file) merged Narau [nxu] into Kaure [bpp]; the only Narau-specific data ever recorded is Giel's 1959 survey wordlist (Nationaal Archief, Den Haag), and Hammarstrom/Palmer judge Narau "not appreciably different to Kaure" (a southern Kaure variety near the Narau river). Every descriptive statement found is about Kaure proper (kaur1271), specifically the Harna/Masta dialect described by Dommel & Dommel (1991). A catalog entry should be filed under kaur1271 (Kaure-Narau), not nara1265.

sources.note: Quotes Dommel & Dommel: stress realised as intensity and tone; always on a high-level or high-mid-falling-tone syllable; single falling tone -> that syllable; two adjacent -> first; non-adjacent -> last primary, rest secondary; stress on high-level-tone syllables unpredictable (phonemic); affixed word main stress on last stressed syllable, up to 4 secondary stresses. Coded primary 'L/LEX (Tone)', secondary i('H,'LL)R.
